chapter: Ellington, the South, bebop and radio
title: Jack Teagarden in Kansas City and Teagarden-style trombone
summary: He met Teagarden at a Kansas City jam, remembers his Dinah solo, and agrees he and Jimmy Harrison both came from Louis.

story.theme_name: Trombonists: who they heard, admired and learned from
story.community_name: Talking trombonists: who played the slide and how

blocks.x: Speaking about Chief reminds a little of Jack Teagarden, maybe because people used to say that Teagarden was part-Indian. But you mentioned once that you ran into him in Kansas City.
I did.
Did you play together then, that time?
Dickenson - 141
We did, you know, a jamming thing, you know. It was just a jam thing, you know.
Did he impress you?
Oh yeah. I had heard him... When I met him, I had heard him on records.
He made a lot of records with Ben Pollack.
Yes.
People used to say that it was amazing (I mean, people who heard both of them) that he and Jimmy Harrison were so similar.
Yeah, they were. Very similar.
And they both... In a way, both came from Louis, I guess.
Oh, sure. He (?)played that way always(?). Teagarden played a solo once that I really liked. That was 'Dinah.'
On the Red Nichols record?
I guess it was.
It's a slow 'Dinah.'
Yes.
Oh yeah.
Yeah.
It's funny, because that was... I got to music, naturally in Europe, through records. And the records were
Dickenson - 142
kind of helter-skelter, because I had to pick up whatever I could find.
Yeah, that was a good method.
And that one was the first time I... I didn't know who Jack Teagarden was, but it had his name on the label as the trombonist. [SILENCE] You mentioned working in Cincinnati with Fats Waller.
